Astra Microwave Expands Counter-UAV Portfolio With “Electromagnetic Wall” Concept
morning.text:
According to what appears on the company’s ongoing counter-drone capabilities, Astra Microwave Products is expanding its Counter-UAVs (C-UAVs) portfolio and is working on new countermeasures for drones to erect a dedicated “electromagnetic wall” against hostile drones. This announcement comes on the heel of India pushing to set up an indigenous capacity in drone detection, prevention, and elimination.
Having a Footprint in Counter-UAVs, Investor material on the counter-drone capabilities of Astra Microwave Products showed “Counter-UAV Systems” and “Drishti counter UAV Radar” are part of the company’s homeland-security and electronics-radar capability. The firm has radar electronics, EW capabilities, and other RF & microwave equipment as features in its Portfolio which could forms some of the foundational technologies in C-UAV, providing layered protection of drones.
Astra stated that it is aiming to boost and customize its Counter-Drone expertise and products into segments that are varying in nature. In an investor call conducted in November 2025 that indicated how many successful counter drone bids and some losses incurred in L2 type competition saw management announce some strategies to further optimize its capabilities while taking note of an upcoming space.
The “electromagnetic wall” concept is crucial considering that modern Counter-UAV Systems are using electronic warfare measures instead of kinetic weapons. An electromagnetic wall could essentially mean a protected area using RF sensing, detect, jamming, and other measures to foil mission accomplished by any foreign drone.
The whole could very likely be a C-UAS System utilizing several protective layers. Firstly, a Radar or other sensing systems can pick up and guide targeting into the rogue drones, and then EW modules can intercept and disable some part of the command line, navigation or other RF dependent technologies. Depending on the nature and threat level in which system is operational, the physical layer can do the task in shape of hard-kill systems.
The microwave and RF electronics firm Astra Microwave has some sort of natural industrial base that it can use in creating any sort of such a systems. The firm designs and manufactures systems for microwave frequencies, which is also extends to radar as well as electronic-warfare and missile related electronics. A C-UAS systems, Counter-UAV Radar, and an Active Array Antenna system could be counted as part of the products listed on the investor presentation of the company.
Astra have stated in the past that they perceive that there will be great opportunity ahead in developing counter drone technology. A study conducted in 2025 on the counter drone market estimates large increment for the market in the domestic Indian scene through the ending of the decade, and lists of Astra Microwave as Indian firms to feature among these markets.
UAV threat evolution is now moving from basic remotely-controlled devices into systems that have built-in-autonomous guided navigation, frequency-hopping methods, secure datalinks and swarm capabilities. Such sophisticated measures could make many conventional RF-based jam machines incapable of stopping such threats, thus making an augmented layered system essential for them.
Thus the importance of electromagnetic “wall”. Such systems, instead of taking each drones individually, a more proficient e-protection mechanism can secure an electronic perimeter that any military command post, air base, critical facility etc can employ around itself. This could prevent the enemy drones coming closer or targeting the area.
The overall performance parameters of the electromagnetically shielded “wall” system, and its architecture that are stated to be developed by Astra Microwave Products, were not given public declaration. Such a system can neither be thought to be developed by Astra yet or made available to markets that require it yet.
However the overall approach of Astra would lean towards a networked layered protection system to counter the drone threat including sensors and electronic-warfare with potential to execute physical destruction. The company has openly admitted dealing with different opportunities available against drones, trying to customize their services to meet the needs of markets that vary greatly.

morning.title: Could an Indian Drone Maker Become India’s Baykar? Mapping the Trajectory
morning.text:
It is very interesting that Turkey’s Baykar has become somewhat of an anomaly in the global defence-industry mythology; a company which has transformed over the last decade from a fairly humble family owned engineering firm to, argueably the worlds most successful drone manufacturer in 10 years due to the success of its Bayraktar TB2 in Libya, Nagorno Karabakh and Ukraine, and has become an aspriational comparison for almost everyserious discussion about India’s new private drone sector. What is far less obvious, is that there seem to be less that look at the structural conditions that underwrite Baykar’s success, and compare it to whether anything existing currently matches the conditions at which it operates.
There were three conditions which created Baykar’s current prominence, which fed into one another to make this development happen: A state that supported Baykar for the long term considering it a strategic national asset even long before it seemed that its systems would ever be able to deliver on any sales commercially, which offered its R&D and procurement guarantee that the TB2 had years before it managed to become something that would sell; genuine, but accidental combat experience, it could never have manufactured that with all the advertising and Indian orders you can throw at it-combat against real air-defense and E-W environments are the best and the last source of credibility from which any client wishes to acquire something from; and finally leadership that possessed the technical backing with sufficient political influence to circumvent all the red tape.
While India has moved forward in the post 2020 trend by liberalising the sectors that can develop this industry even now being able to bypass a lot of import restriction factors and even open it for non-DPSU bodies, has resulted in a much wider variety of private players that didn’t have so much attention before; such as ideaForge with their public record on the stock exchange since 2023, with a massive client base both in Indian security agencies and across international export customers.
Nevertheless there are not enough customers outside India willing to pay for loitering munitions and large unmanned aircraft considering Operation Sindoor had to be bought in due to some urgent requirement, and they do not have the second component which allows these drone manufacturing companies to operate such that of what happened with Baykar where its marketing claims turned into established fact due to actual field combat verification, it really doesn’t matter how many years and what amount of resources a company has invested till it sees what is does to an actual E-W & air defense environment.
The importance of comparing India’s efforts with Baykar stems at the policy level and thus suggests two areas they actually can affect, not the first two that don’t depend on state backing as much or don’t necessarily relate to them: First, patient support for its chosen privately developed drone manufacturers like a nation views a strategic national asset, not an individual vendor in a tender competition that is based on the cheapest unit price.
Second, export clearance processes that will expedite to the approval rate seen with regards to bringing successful Indian designed hardware to international clients, rather than having it screened thoroughly over time to guarantee safety. What hasn’t occurred to us is that while we want to achieve what Baykar has done in Turkey, our nation should work to achieve those two aspects mentioned earlier rather than trying to manufacture the impossible as in giving rise to Operation Sindoor (not really an operation where drones proved their viability against superior tech), so India can create its very own Indian Baykar through these means.

morning.title: How India Can Sell More BrahMos: The Roadmap to a $5 Billion Missile Export Empire
morning.text:
With three customers signed on and six more in line to join them, the world is ready for some non-Chinese and non-Western precision strike capability. The Brahmos is now the only supersonic cruise missile for sale to anyone, anywhere in the world. The world wants in and here’s how India can turn a missile that had zero buyers up until 2022 into a 5 billion dollar export franchise.
It’s been a quick flip. Until 2022 it had zero foreign customers; today its got three contracted clients-Philippines, Vietnam and Indonesia and active negotiations with the UAE and interest from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Thailand, Brazil, Chile, South Africa and others to purchase. Already a significant contributor with the defense export numbers jumping 62 percent last fiscal to 38,424 crore making it India’s flag-bearer in defense exports, India targets 50,000crore in annual defense exports by 2029.
The Prospective Customer Map
| Region | Country | Strategic Driver | Status | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Southeast Asia | Philippines | South China Sea dispute with China | Delivered (2024) | 
| Southeast Asia | Vietnam | South China Sea dispute; China antagonism | Signed (2026) | 
| Southeast Asia | Indonesia | South China Sea; Natuna Islands | MoU signed, contracts follow | 
| Southeast Asia | Malaysia | South China Sea dispute | Interest expressed | 
| Southeast Asia | Thailand | Maritime security modernisation | Interest expressed | 
| Middle East | UAE | Post-Iran conflict; Strait of Hormuz; reduce Western dependence | Active negotiations | 
| Middle East | Saudi Arabia | Counter Iran; Saudi-Pakistan pact reshaping alliances | Interest expressed | 
| Middle East | Egypt | Regional power projection | Interest expressed | 
| Middle East | Oman | Strait of Hormuz security | Discussed | 
| South America | Brazil | Defence modernisation; non-aligned posture | Interest expressed | 
| South America | Chile | Coastal defence modernisation | Interest expressed | 
| South America | Argentina | Defence budget constraints; affordable option | Discussed | 
| Africa | South Africa | Regional power projection; IBSA ties | Interest expressed | 
| Europe | Bulgaria | Reported in potential future acquisition discussions | Preliminary | 
| Eurasia | Russia | Ukraine war depletion; JV partner; potential extended-range variant | Under consideration | 
Five Strategies to Scale BrahMos Exports:
1. Tackle the Lifecycle Support Gap- The biggest hurdle identified by The Diplomat is the lack of foreign maintenance hubs, logistics networks and after sales support. The US and France provide institutional support for trained technicians, spare parts, and warranty-centric upgrades while India’s export structure continues to be a piecemeal delivery approach that focuses merely on the hardware. The UAE and Indonesia, as example with their diverse defense inventory need assurance and a plan to ensure BrahMos fits seamlessly within their current command and control infrastructure. India would have to create offshore maintenance, assembly and repair locations in Southeast Asia, the Gulf and also potentially in Africa, ensuring that trained operators are at hand along with spare parts for steady continuity-else future deals, replenishment and repeat business might be jeopardized.
2. Broaden customer base via BrahMos-NG- The current Brahmos is about three tonnes and thus only can be launched from heavyweight assets like shore based batteries, capital warships and large Sukhoi fighter jet aircraft. At a lightweight 1.2 tones, BrahMos-NG has the advantage of being able to launch from virtually any aircraft type-Tejas fighters, Rafael, light and medium weight frigates and even patrol boats. This doubles/triples the market of the Brahmos as the potential clientele would include countries with smaller navies and weaker fighter aircraft assets like Malaysia, Thailand, Argentina and South Africa to purchase the missile. A deal of up to 20 percent cut down in production costs is anticipated in two years as part of developing the BrahMos-NG; something that would put it in the reach of these governments.
3. Offer composite solutions with Akash steer and Astra- The days of sing-product deals were a thing of the past. The deal with Indonesia includes the air-to-air Astra missile for theirSu-30 fleet in addition to Brahmos missile and also a pact to co-develop Sabang-Aceh Port adjacent to the Malacca Strait. Similarly, UAE talks also envision combined sale of Brahmos with the Akashsteer air defense control and command system.
Layered defense deals that include cruise missiles and air defense, plus the possibility to purchase an air-to-air missile option, not only ups the deal values, but also creates diplomatic entrapment; something where competitive pressure becomes minimal. Armenia recently purchased Akash missile systems, Pinaka rocket launchers and 155mm artillery rounds simultaneously, showcasing such possible bundled deals.
4. Put in place a defense export financing framework- For nations likeArgentina, South Africa, and Chile whose defense budgets are stretched, financing will be the crucial missing link that France (via export guarantees), the USA (Foreign Military Financing) and Russia (via rupee denomination in ruble-based barter and loan schemes) already provide. The Exim Bank of India could provide line-of-credit for purchasing Brahmos systems backed by government guarantee with either deferred payment, bartering against indigenous goods, or leasing options allowing smaller economies the breathing room they require.
5. Eliminate Russia Veto Bottleneck- Every single third-country Brahmos acquisition contract needs endorsement from the Russian government under the50.5/49.5JV arrangement. Although Moscow granted its approval for Vietnam and Indonesia these deals were somewhat stretched due to a protracted consultation process, and similar approvals might turn tricky in countries where Indian and Russian national interests may clash. A pre-approval understanding with the Russia under some form of standard protocol would ensure smooth transaction and diplomatic leverage, with the potential Russian purchase for their depleted navy being an opening.
The Revenue Opportunity-
Considering that even 5 of these 10+ interested countries make it to contracted customers with average order size of $300-600M per country over the coming ten years, Brahmos could net $3-5 billion for India. Coupled with increased sales through BrahMos-NG’s introduction to the market, bigger deals with composite solution sales, and recurring maintenance revenue, the Brahmos franchise alone is pegged to account for 20-30 per cent of India’s targeted $50,000 crore defense exports by 2029. The missile with no customer till 2022 could very well end up being the singular biggest defense export item from India by 2030.

morning.title: Why HAL Must Risk Designing Its Own Sixth-Generation Fighter Or Permanently Lose The Future Of Combat Aircraft Production
morning.text:
India’s next three decades at the forefront of combat aircraft production is balanced on a knife edge; either Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) remains as India’s foremost fighter builder, or will be reduced to merely a licensed production agency of other people’s designs. HAL’s exclusion from the new fifth-generation fighter programme – which has now seen the involvement of three private-sector consortia bidding for prototype development in tandem with ADA – indicates more than simple procurement, its a warning to HAL from the MOD to not assume monopoly production of fighters, and a commitment by the MoD to begin building rival capability in the private-sector. Failure to initiate a sixth-generation fighter design programme would relegate HAL to a history production house for variants of the Tejas and licensed helicopters forever.
Reasoning for this was explained clearly by the defence secretary: nearly all major foreign defense producers operate with two fighter production lines operated by two different companies and that too few opportunities to bet against a single design is a poor way to go. While this is a logical stance, it is unfortunate given HAL’s context, HAL has guaranteed orders for another decade and a half, in part with one hundred and eighty Tejas Mk1A fighters as well as order for LCA Mk2 development and helicopter production contracts. However with LCA Mk2 production scheduled only for 2029 at the earliest and HAL having nothing on the production side beyond it the exclusion from the AMCA-a clear program of the future generation of fighter aircraft-along with talks about the next sixth-gen fighter program with European conglomerates, suggests a deliberate action on the part of the government.
If HAL aims to survive as a combat aircraft designer as opposed to a mere production agency then the only path available is immediately undertake an independent sixth-generation fighter study program; this doesn’t necessarily need to go as far as to build an independently designed prototype with limited resources and funding on its own-which is probably just as feasible an endeavor as to build even the simplest contemporary military design on a comparable scale like Lockheed Martin or Dassault is for a similar objective –as it requires HAL to spend its own internal R&D funds for design study concept related to a 6th generation airframe based on its own experiences with the LCA’s and LCAMk2, and on its capacity as part of Indian-French collaboration to work on the 5th generation program as opposed to expecting the Government of India give its a 6th generation Fighter program in a while. It already possesses fundamental knowledge of air-frame structures, design of integrated avionics system as well as flight control, and has proved its design capabilities for developing original indigenous hardware for its own fighters (RS422 and optical fluid sensing now in use on LCA Mk2.)
The opportunity cost is all in the other direction: should the AMCA and the 6th Gen Euro-partnered projects continue without HAL the defense ministry will continue to award new contracts and contracts for future platforms like the LCAMk2 fighters but only to the private sector now that HAL is not involved in building this aircraft of the future at the early concept and design stages. HAL’s engineering teams would lose access to invaluable knowledge and experiences relating to new fighter designs, a knowledge and information base painstakingly cultivated over half-a-century, which would mean that any future project for new fighter aircraft that HAL wants to bid for it must also secure design-sharing for itself or it would essentially find itself at the receiving end of design specifications and information as a production partner. The claim made that HAL does not possess any useful technological capacity to independently pursue 6th Generation Design Program is incorrect because although an independent program will undoubtedly have overlapping requirements, the ultimate design will reflect the unique doctrine, technology available in India and specific needs of the Indian military-which can only be realized through designing and prototyping within India by a company such as HAL-as compared to the alternative, a design built on European specifications by one or more major foreign aerospace companies.

morning.title: Saab Wins ₹472 Crore Deal for 450 Carl-Gustaf M4
morning.text:
Saab’s FFV Ordnance has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for the Indian Army’s procurement of 450 Carl-Gustaf M4 rocket launchers. Quoting at ₹471.87 crore for the requirement, the firm’s proposal was selected as part of the Army’s effort to acquire lighter, more versatile shoulder-fired weapons to update its firepower.
The proposed procurement includes 450 Carl-Gustaf M4 launchers, along with accessories, spares, training and support requirements. The Army had placed the requirement under the Buy (Indian) category, and expected to manufacture the systems indigenously. Saab’s Jhajjar facility will become the first Carl-Gustaf manufacturing base outside Sweden. Having received approval for 100% foreign direct investment, the Swedish firm has stated it will work with Indian suppliers, as part of its Make in India strategy.
The Carl-Gustaf M4 is the latest-generation 84mm recoilless weapon from Saab. Weighing in at around 6.6–7 kg without sights and accessories, the system is much lighter than earlier variants, and is ideal for infantry carrying it over extended operations. The Army’s requirement includes compatibility with modern sighting systems, including digital fire-control devices, and red-dot sights, to aid target-acquisition and first-round hit probability.
The launcher also features Picatinny rails and improved ergonomics. The L1 status is yet another feather in the cap for Saab’s growing manufacturing footprint in India. The firm has previously stated that its Jhajjar facility will employ advanced manufacturing technologies, including carbon-fibre winding and modern sighting technology, while working with Indian sub-suppliers.

morning.title: IITK RaSET Pinaka Rocket Reaches 85 Metres After Anomaly terminated flight
morning.text:
The IITK Rocketry and Space Exploration Team (IITK RaSET) recently launched the latest in its experimental rocket series, Pinaka. However, the flight had to be terminated prematurely due to a malfunction in one of the stages.
The launch – which was carried out on August 30 and had a planned apogee of 1 km – saw the rocket reaching around 85 metres before the incident. Nevertheless, the team remarked that the launch provided the members with much needed engineering and field-testing experience. According to the team, the commercial rocket motor used in the flight malfunctioned, causing the flight to terminate early.
The forward closure of the motor – which kept the motor chamber sealed – failed to hold during the flight and slid upwards. The team further added that the hot gases escaping the motor chamber cut through the avionics bay of the rocket, bringing it to an end. Despite the propulsion failure, the team noted that the components that it designed, manufactured and tested worked according to expectations during the initial phase of the flight.
These consisted of the rocket’s airframe, fins and structural integration. According to the team, the rocket maintained its structural integrity throughout until the departure from the pad when the propulsion malfunction took over. One of the positive outcomes of the flight for the team was the performance of the rocket’s telemetry system.
Although the team stated that much of the onboard electronics were damaged due to the fire, the telemetry system continued recording and relaying key pre-failure flight data to the ground station.
The data can be crucial for post-flight analysis by the team to help them understand the progression of the incident leading to the flight termination.

morning.text:
An obscure photograph is circulating among the Indian defence enthusiasts that has become related to one of the most gruesome and disputed incidents attributed to India’s Special Forces. Shared online often as an “Ghost Paltan” picture (a popular name attributed to a group of commandos that features an image and a text written in it), the wall displays an barely visible Hindi phrase “Hum shikari hain, dushman hai shikar; hinsa ke hum malik hain, tum bas kirayedaar” meaning “We are the hunters; enemy, the prey; we command violence, your entry merely on rental”.
On social media this picture is often shared in relation to a post-border raid conducted by India’s Special Forces, retaliating against the killing of the Pakistani forces. According to a version of the narrative commonly spread by enthusiasts and defence websites, this operation was carried out in order to punish the killing and maltreatment of Captain Saurabh Kalia and 5 troopers of the 4 Jat regime during the Kargil conflict. The Six personnel captured along with Captain Saurabh Kalia in the Kaksar sector on May 15, 1999 were held hostage by the Pakistani soldiers for a duration of 22 days before their mutilated corpses returned in India.
As claimed by accounts from Indian side, Captain Saurabh Kalia and soldiers were subjected to inhumane torture. Subsequently called a barbaric act by the Indian government, the incident was taken up with the United Nations.
The exact details about the photograph however, aren’t as clearly ascertained as their popularity. According to a legend linked to the photograph, the photograph depicts a post-border operation carried out by a unit of Indian Special Forces who ambushed a position manned by Pakistan Army, killings 22 troopers. It’s alleged that “Hum shikari hain…” were written using the blood of those killed with some versions asserting the existence of a particular officer from Pakistani administration allegedly responsible for their torture captured and eliminated along with the troop; and that this operative had been under radar for ages through intelligence.
There however doesn’t exist any solid public evidence that may independently verify these facts of a post-border strike by an unknown SAS contingent at a Pakistani Army post on a wall displaying the given Hindi poem in blood of martyred Pakistani troop. A thread in Reddit, for instance stated almost the same story but also contained confusion about the Indian outfit and operations’ real aim. These specific facts of “Ghost Paltan”, about the 22-member Pakistani Army troop’s mortality and identification of the key person allegedly responsible for Capt.
That detail of the operation becomes important because Indian Special Forces operate covertly and facts regarding their missions often undergo an imaginative evolution over the passage of time. Separately, there exists uncertainty about Operation Apache being another such operation. It still needs verification as the operations details were different depending upon whichever online discussions on Reddit.
Captain Kalia’s capture and death along the LoC after a fighting engagement turned into a significant landmark case about what should or should not be done, where Captain Saurabh Kalia and 5 soldiers fought valiantly but surrendered due to lack of ammunition. The deceased are remembered in India as brave soldiers and there has been a protracted attempt by their families and nation at large to recognize their demise as a war crime. Thus, the ghost Paltan is a controversial narrative that stands between a recorded military fact and the legend of Special Forces, their messages serving as symbol for the retaliatory instincts assumed by these units however, certain spectacular elements around photograph might have no substantial proofs to validate it.

India targets a five-fold increase in its global space economy share over the next 10 years, says Indian media: This involves India expanding its slice of the international space economy from its current 2-2.5% to 8-10%.
The space industry has seen at least five or six private players launch their own satellites in communication, ISR and beyond. And the space economy could grow to $44 billion, thanks to an expected boost in agricultural and disaster management, as well as healthcare.
In space, India accounts for only about 2-3% of the global space economy at present. It intends to increase this to around 8% by 2030. Government calculations estimates the space economy to be about $44 billion by 2033, about 8% of the estimated global market then.
From an lone registered space startup in 2014, India now has above 400; even government estimates state more than 440 startups by 2026, with private firms now designing and building vehicles, satellites and observational systems, propulsion units, and space services, among others.
The Space-sector vision of India has outlined Space-for-Earth applications-communications, remote sensing, navigation, weather services, data-based services among other-as a massive segment. Achieving the $40-45 billion figures would demand indigenous players to scale up from experiments to fully commercial models. Policy reforms already paving the way forprivate playersand establishment of IN-SPACe to both streamline as well as promote activities in this domain; the policy also envisages to bring about change by increasing foreign investments both in terms of technology and finance. It is no longer enough to build satellites and launch them into space.
Instead, the dream now is to design, develop, build, launch, operate and sell space technologies and services globally through indigenous enterprises.

morning.title: ISRO staff bodies seek clarification on trajectory of privatisation
morning.text:
Nine employee associations at the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) have written to the space agency’s Chairperson V Narayanan, seeking official clarification on the proposed transfer of its manufacturing and operational functions to private entities.
In a letter, dated September 4, the associations also raised questions about the agency’s future role, and the consequences for serving employees and future recruitment.
“Private participation in defined commercial activities can coexist with a strong, publicly owned ISRO. What cannot be accepted without debate is a policy that reduces ISRO to a residual R&D (research and development) boutique while the realisation of the nation’s launch vehicles and the operation of its launch infrastructure pass out of public hands,” the letter said.
It pointed to the August 21 comments made by Pawan Goenka, chairperson of the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorisation Centre (IN-SPACe), which promotes, enables, authorises and supervises various space activities of non-governmental entities.
Goenka, at a public event, reportedly said, “Eventually, ISRO will not make any launch vehicles and will not manufacture any launch vehicles. That will all be done by the private sector or PSU.” The employee associations claimed that these remarks have not been accompanied by any corresponding official communication from the Department of Space, explaining the approved policy, its legal and administrative basis, its phasing, or its consequences for the existing workforce and future public recruitment.
“Technology developed by ISRO is a national asset. Its transfer must be transparent, accountable and consistent with strategic, safety and employment considerations — not presented to employees through newspaper reports,” the letter said.
It raised several other concerns. These include whether the design, development, realisation, integration, testing and launch of PSLV, LVM3, SSLV and successor vehicles will continue as ISRO functions or will cease.
Also, it asked about the implications of the proposed shift for sanctioned strength, existing vacancies, recruitment calendar, and induction of scientific/technical/administrative/industrial manpower in all ISRO centres.

morning.title: Turkey Claims its ALP-300G Radar is Better then S-400 Radar
morning.text:
One more piece of “progress” from Turkey’s indigenous air defence industry, with an ASELSAN engineer telling Al Jazeera that the ALP-300G radar, developed for the planned Turkish long-range air defence architecture, out-performs Russia’s S-400 search radar in multiple domains.
The claim is important as the Russian S-400 was contracted by Turkey in 2017 (resulting in Ankara being kicked out of the F-35 program and American sanctions imposed upon it), and its replacement or supplementation through locally manufactured items represents an interesting facet of Turkey’s indigenous technology endeavors. The ALP-300G is an S-band AESA early warning radar from ASELSAN; this radar’s capabilities, according to the company, include multi-channel receivers with digital beam-forming allowing for the development of multi-mission radar systems producing multiple simultaneous beams. The ALP-300G claims that the radar can detect a range of targets including low-RCS and stealth types, anti-radiation missiles, and ballistic missiles.
Also of note, is the radar’s claimed ability to provide its 3D air-picture information for other radars and command centres in an integrated air defense picture. In an Al Jazeera program that covers the ALP-300G, the engineer is asked to contrast the radar with its Russian S-400 equivalent. The engineer claimed the ALP-300G out performs the S-400 search radar in “multiple ways”.
We would present the claim as an industry report rather than verified performance information. Neither ASELSAN’s public specifications nor public domain Russian parameters confirm that the ALP-300G provides categorically superior performance across all parameters to the S-400’s search radar. In addition to comparing the radar to that of the S-400, the engineer was also questioned regarding the use of any foreign supplied parts in the system, in which the answer received is arguably very important; the engineer confidently states that not only the system in itself but every constituent electronic chip was developed in Turkey from beginning to end.
ASELSAN also states that it has been producing Domestic GaN transistors for its S-band systems (and that they are still in process of doing so in the annual report of 2023).
The S-400 acquisition, is of critical import as it lead to significant rupture with Washington and Turkey’s expulsion from the F-35 program. This issue has resulted in considerable investment in sensors, command and control systems, missiles and air defense equipment within Turkey’s domestic industry.

morning.title: UN-backed proposed world map must depict J-K, Ladakh as per India’s official map: MEA
morning.text:
India on Sunday said a UN-initiated proposed world map must depict Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh in accordance with the country’s official map, and any “inaccurate” or “misleading” representation will be unacceptable.
New Delhi’s assertion came two days after it voted in favour of a UN General Assembly resolution aimed at correcting the world map to promote a more accurate representation of continental landmasses. The resolution titled “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa” was adopted on September 4.
External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India highlighted that the resolution does not constitute endorsement of any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries.
“India voted in favour of the resolution and also made an explanation of vote stressing on the underlying principle of promoting equal – area cartographic representation,” he said.
Jaiswal was responding to a media query on the issue.
“India’s sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India’s official map. Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable,” he said.
“Our position on India’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable,” he noted.
Jaiswal said the purpose of the UN resolution is “to encourage the use of equal-area map projections that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses.”
“The resolution neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names,” he said.
The resolution, sponsored by Togo, received 164 votes in favour, with abstentions from Estonia, Georgia, Lithuania, Moldova, Serbia and Ukraine, and a lone vote against from the United States.

morning.title: Jaishankar pays tribute to Indian rulers who sheltered Polish refugees during WWII
morning.text:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday visited two memorials in Warsaw that commemorate India’s humanitarian role in providing shelter to Polish refugees during World War II, recalling a little-known chapter that continues to shape the close ties between the two countries.
Jaishankar’s visit to the memorials came a day after he held wide-ranging talks with Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski on Friday, covering trade and investment, defence, space, artificial intelligence, semiconductors, energy and supply-chain resilience.
Jaishankar is on a two-nation visit to Ukraine and Poland from September 3-5. He visited Kyiv on Thursday, where he held talks with top Ukrainian leadership.
At the memorial of Maharaja Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja of Nawanagar, Jaishankar recalled the words with which the Indian ruler welcomed Polish children who had fled the devastation of the war: “I am Bapu, the father of all Nawanagaris, including yourselves.”
In a post on X, Jaishankar on Saturday said Jadeja was “fondly remembered for looking after 1,000 Polish children during World War II” and that his “warmth and compassion remain an abiding bridge” between India and Poland.
Jadeja, the ruler of the erstwhile princely state of Nawanagar, now part of Gujarat’s Jamnagar, provided shelter and care to the children at a settlement in Balachadi. The children were provided accommodation, food, education and medical care, and came to remember him as their “Bapu”, or father.
Jadeja, also referred to as Jam Saheb, is popularly remembered in Poland as the “Dobry Maharaja (Good King)”. His memorial is situated in Warsaw’s Ochota district and is known as the Square of the Good Maharaja.
Jaishankar visited the memorial on Saturday along with Polish MP Kinga Gajewska and Ochota Mayor Piotr Krasnodębski. The external affairs minister later paid his respects at the Kolhapur Memorial in Warsaw, which commemorates another chapter of India’s wartime assistance to Poland.
The memorial recalls the refuge provided by the princely state of Kolhapur to around 5,000 Polish refugees, including women and children, who were sheltered at Valivade near Kolhapur in Maharashtra during World War II.
“This act of generosity is still fresh in the memory of the Polish people,” Jaishankar said in another post on X, recalling the refuge provided to the Polish refugees.
The two memorials are part of a wider historical connection that has gained renewed attention in India-Poland relations in recent years.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi had visited both memorials during his Poland visit in August 2024, highlighting the wartime stories as an important link between the two countries.During his current visit, Jaishankar announced that the second edition of the Jam Saheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme would take place in October.
The programme was launched after Modi’s 2024 visit and is aimed at bringing Polish youth to India to learn about the history of the Polish refugee settlements in Balachadi and Valivade.
The two sides on Friday discussed the war in Ukraine, the situation in West Asia and the Indo-Pacific. Jaishankar said India and Poland, as political democracies and open market economies, could cooperate on major global issues.
He said the two countries were also working on agreements in areas including cybersecurity, space, clean coal, classified information and critical minerals.

morning.title: Rising peptide use sparks safety concerns
morning.text: New Delhi: Doctors have raised concerns over the growing popularity of injectable peptides for weight loss, muscle recovery, anti-ageing and longevity, warning that the success of a few scientifically established peptide medicines should not be confused with the safety or efficacy of experimental compounds being promoted online.The concerns have come into focus after a proposed "Peptide Party" in Bengaluru was cancelled following regulatory intervention, highlighting a wider trend of people exploring peptide-based therapies outside conventional medical settings.Peptides are short chains of amino acids that act as signalling molecules in the body. While medicines such as insulin and GLP-1-based drugs have well-established medical applications, several compounds popular in the biohacking and longevity space have limited human evidence.Also read: RPG Life Sciences to deploy Rs 500 crore in next 12 months to bolster manufacturing, API capabilitiesDr Naval K Vikram, professor in the Department of Medicine at AIIMS, Delhi and an expert in metabolic disorders, said the growing interest in peptides needed to be viewed with caution, particularly when consumers begin to equate all peptides with established drugs.He emphasised that they should not be used without medical supervision."Peptides are not one homogeneous group of medicines. Some have undergone extensive clinical research and are routinely used in medicine, while others are still experimental."The fact that semaglutide or another peptide-based drug works does not mean that every peptide being sold for weight loss, muscle recovery or longevity will have the same safety and efficacy," Vikram said.He said the use of such compounds should be guided by quality of evidence, regulatory status and the patient's individual medical condition rather than social media claims or anecdotal experiences.Aman Puri, founder of sports and wellness brand, Steadfast Nutrition, said the growing influence of social media influencers, celebrities and the wellness industry has made consumers increasingly willing to experiment with injectable and unapproved peptides promising greater longevity, sharper cognition and better sleep.Also read: Seized Abhayrab vials not manufactured by company: Indian Immunologicals Limited"The larger concern is when wellness trends start replacing evidence-based decision making. Consumers need to understand what they are taking, why they are taking it and whether there is credible human evidence behind the claim," Puri said.He said the quality and source of a product were equally important, particularly when it involved injectable preparations. Such products should only be taken if prescribed by a doctor and under medical supervision."While the safety and efficacy of certain oral peptide supplements is supported by research, these should not be treated as substitutes for a balanced diet and should be taken after consultation with a healthcare professional," Puri stated.Dr Ravinder Goswami, professor in the Endocrinology at AIIMS, Delhi, said the biggest misconception was that the word "peptide" itself represented a guarantee of safety."Peptide is a chemical and biological category, not a certificate of safety. Two peptides can have completely different mechanisms, indications, doses and adverse-effect profiles. A compound that looks promising in laboratory or animal studies cannot automatically be recommended for use in humans," the senior endocrinologist said.Goswami said self-injection was particularly concerning as users may not know whether a product contains the stated compound or concentration and may also mishandle storage, dilution or administration."Once an experimental compound is injected, you are exposing the entire body to it. With products that lack adequate human safety data, we may simply not know the consequences of prolonged use or of combining several such compounds," he said.He also cautioned against "peptide stacking", in which people combine multiple compounds based on recommendations circulating in online fitness and biohacking communities.Functional medicine practitioner Mugdha Pradhan, founder of iThrive, a health and wellness company, said the peptide conversation should not be reduced to a simple question of whether peptides were "good" or "bad"."There is genuine science behind peptide biology and there are peptide therapies with important clinical applications. But the conversation needs to move beyond marketing and ask what evidence exists for a particular peptide, what problem it is being used for and whether its use is appropriate for that individual," she said.Pradhan said consumers should also be wary of treating emerging therapies as quick fixes for complex metabolic or ageing-related problems.The Bengaluru episode has highlighted how rapidly the peptide conversation is moving from specialist medical settings into the wider wellness ecosystem.Doctors said the popularity of semaglutide and tirzepatide had likely contributed to the perception that "peptides" were synonymous with weight loss and rapid health benefits. However, established drugs have gone through clinical trials, regulatory scrutiny, quality-controlled manufacturing and post-marketing monitoring, they noted.Experts said consumers considering peptide-based treatment should therefore consult a qualified doctor and verify the product's regulatory status, source, composition and intended indication rather than relying on influencers, online communities or anecdotal success stories.

morning.title: U.S. Navy Accelerates Tomahawk Production Citing ‘Current International Conflict’
morning.text:
The U.S. Navy is rapidly accelerating Tomahawk cruise missile production to meet urgent inventory demands, leveraging a legacy 2019 SLAM-ER contract to fast-track new warhead casings by 2027.

Tomahawk production is slated to receive a major boost with a new production modification tacked onto an existing 2019 contract for SLAM-ER cruise missiles. The move, detailed in a Sept. 2 contract notice, cites immediate demand for increased production as the primary reason for the acceleration.

“The tasking in the proposed modification provides for [General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems] to manufacture and deliver [redacted] warhead housings, within nine months, to be used in the production of missile warhead sections for the U/RGM-109E TACTOM,” the document reads. “This accelerated delivery schedule is due to immediate demand for increased missile production for the United States Navy, as a result of current international conflict.”

General Dynamics builds warhead casings for both SLAM-ER and Tactical Tomahawks for the U.S. Navy.

The U.S. Navy has fired hundreds of Tomahawk cruise missiles at targets in Iran since the start of Operation Epic Fury. Concerns over remaining stockpiles have dominated conversations around the United States’ ability to sustain a wider conflict if one were to occur, most notably in the Indo-Pacific. The Pentagon has already signed frameworks with major defense companies—some contingent on congressional funding—to accelerate the production of other key expended munitions, including the Navy’s SM-3 anti-ballistic missile and the Army’s PAC-3 MSE interceptor.

The move to fold Tomahawk warhead production into SLAM-ER production is another case of accelerated manufacturing supporting inventory replenishment across major U.S. military weapon systems. The newly delivered warheads will be installed on both newly built and recertified Block IV/V Tomahawk missiles.

“In order to meet the required delivery date of the first assets, the Government needs [first article inspections] to begin no later than [the] 1st Quarter of calendar year 2027,” the contract adds. “GD-OTS has the requisite knowledge, expertise and technical experience to meet this urgent missile delivery schedule.”

Tacking Tomahawk casing production onto the existing SLAM-ER contract avoids the long lead times required to award a new contract or qualify a secondary warhead source, granting the U.S. Navy and prime contractor Raytheon faster access to critical subcomponents.

Naval News reached out to the U.S. Navy and General Dynamics for comment, but neither responded prior to publication.

morning.title: German company becomes first in Europe to launch fully commercial orbital rocket
morning.text:
Isar Aerospace, founded in 2018 by three students at a German university, successfully launched a privately-developed rocket into low-Earth orbit Saturday from a Norwegian spaceport inside the Arctic Circle.

The two-stage rocket, named Spectrum, became the first fully commercial launch vehicle in Europe to reach orbit. With Saturday's success, Isar is the clear leader among a pack of several European launch startups vying to inject some competition into Europe's stagnant launch market.

Isar's 92-foot-tall (28-meter) Spectrum rocket lifted off at 4:12 pm EST (20:12 UTC) Saturday from Andøya Spaceport in northern Norway, where it was 10:12 pm local time as the final bluish hues of daylight faded from the late summer sky. Seven minutes later, the rocket was in orbit.

Time lords prepare to kick leap seconds into the next millennium
morning.text: The prospect of a negative leap second – combined with decades of irritation over leap seconds generally – looks set to inspire a bit of global procrastination among international timekeepers. Next month, the General Conference on Weights and Measures is set to vote on effectively calling time on leap seconds. A draft resolution [PDF] would make Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) continuous from May 20, 2027, and allow the difference between UTC and UT1, a measure of time based on Earth's rotation, to reach as much as one hour. Leap seconds keep UTC, which is based on atomic clocks, within 0.9 seconds of time determined by the slightly wobbly rotation of our home planet. Since the system was introduced in 1972, 27 leap seconds have been added to UTC. The urgency comes partly from a slight increase in Earth's rotational speed in recent years, raising the possibility of an adjustment never attempted before: a negative leap second. Experts convened by international timekeeping bodies estimated a 30 percent probability that one would be needed by 2035. Many computer systems were designed on the assumption that a leap second would always be added rather than removed, explained Setnam Shemar, principal scientist at the UK's National Physical Laboratory (NPL). "Most digital architectures and network time servers are hardcoded under the assumption that leap seconds are strictly additive. Losing a second could trigger severe disruption across critical national infrastructure, including telecommunications, electricity grids, and satellite navigation systems," he said. The risks posed by a negative leap second – and leap seconds generally – are behind the proposal to let UTC diverge from rotational time by as much as an hour, which is due to be put to a vote in October. Shemar said the proposal would remove the need for further leap-second adjustments for many years. "This would remove the risks entirely for a very long time. Next month's resolution is likely to pass since it will be based on the outcome of a majority vote of the national delegates from many different countries, and most of them have been keen to end leap seconds for several years due to the risks posed to national infrastructure." UTC would be unlikely to diverge from rotational time by a full hour for at least a thousand years, Shemar said. If humankind lasts that long, it might be the least of our worries. ®

morning.title: US troops can still be tracked by purchased location data, and Congress wants to know why
morning.text: The US military's effort to prevent troops from being tracked by adversaries through purchased location data hasn't worked as well as anticipated, and lawmakers want to know why. US Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-NC) on Friday asked for an investigation by the Defense Department Inspector General into policies that have only partially stanched the flow of location data that allows military personnel to be tracked and targeted. In May, Wyden, Harrigan, and a bipartisan group of 12 other members of Congress released details about how commercially purchased location data – often captured by mobile apps and advertising SDKs – can be used to identify where US military personnel gather and to target those locations. They noted that the DoD has been aware of this threat since at least 2016. The lawmakers urged Defense Department CIO Kirsten A. Davies to take steps to mitigate this risk, including turning off advertising identifiers on DoD smartphones and issuing a policy requiring the disabling of advertising identifiers on all personal devices brought into DoD facilities or overseas. Since then, various military branches have blocked advertising identifiers on government-issued devices. According to the letter, "several DoD components – the Army, Air Force, Navy and Marine Corps, and Special Operations Command – confirm that they now disable advertising IDs on government-issued devices to protect their personnel from such threats." But that hasn't entirely eliminated the availability of location data tied to US military personnel. Citing ongoing reports, Wyden and Harrigan want to know why location data pinpointing the movement of troops continues to be available. "We commend these service branches for implementing this cybersecurity defensive best practice on government devices," they said in their letter [PDF] to the DoD IG. "However, recent reports regarding the continued availability of commercial location data originating from DoD facilities raise troubling questions." The two lawmakers speculate about the reason DoD policies have fallen short. One possibility, they say, is that some parts of the DoD turned off their advertising identifiers only as recently as July. Another, they say, is that disabling ad identifiers may no longer be sufficient to limit the availability of location data. And the third is that the location data is coming entirely from the personal devices of DoD personnel and contractors. Zach Edwards, staff threat researcher at Infoblox, told The Register in an email that it's good to hear all the military branches have disabled advertising IDs on their phones because it will make members of the military and their families safer, especially those serving in combat zones overseas. "This change will essentially ensure that military device location data isn't being included in bulk data sales being done by numerous vendors," he said. "It’s truly unfortunate that Google and Apple have not effectively reformed their mobile advertising IDs, even after it’s been well documented that it’s the primary piece of data being used by data brokers to connect up people’s mobile phone location data for bulk sales." Mobile advertising identifiers (MAIDs), Edwards explained, serve as join keys for tracking people – they can link different datasets. "So one core benefit is that military data won't be available for sale via data brokers, who will sell to literally anyone with a pulse and a credit card," said Edwards. "But the other slightly less obvious benefit is that this MAID was also being broadcast to all ad systems participating in the auctions." Edwards said that while states like California, Vermont, Texas, and Oregon have data broker registries, he's unaware of any Russian or Chinese ad tech vendors who have registered. And those companies, he said, partner with Western publishers and mobile apps to collect data anyway. "I think it's important to appreciate that these ad tech companies in Russia and China have also likely been getting MAID data from the programmatic ad tech auctions from members of the military, and companies in those countries have an obligation to share it with the state without any ability to appeal or provide any external notice," he said. ®
